title: Which smaller copy of the tiger picture keeps its shape?
description: Two copies of a tiger picture are compared with the original, side by side. The video divides each new side by the old side to get the factor of change for the width and for the height. Keeko's doubt is that taking the same length off both sides keeps the shape.
teaching_notes: One idea: a copy keeps the shape when the width and the height are multiplied by the same factor. Watch for students who think that taking the same length off both sides keeps the shape.

source: Image A is 60 mm wide and 40 mm high. Image C is 30 mm by 20
video_script.why: The child sees that a resized picture keeps its shape only when both sides change by one factor, not by one length taken away.
video_script.substitution: Divide each new side by the old side to get a factor, then compare the two factors of each copy.
video_script.anchor: the book's tiger pictures: image A, and the copies B and C
video_script.wrong_answer: both sides lost the same twenty millimetres
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says image B keeps the shape because both sides lost the same twenty millimetres. The height is one half of the old height but the width is only two thirds of the old width, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Image C changed both sides by one half, so it keeps the shape.

final_answer.spoken: image C, with the factor one half

maths_rules: image A: 60 mm wide, 40 mm high
image C: 30 mm by 20 mm; 30 ÷ 60 = 1/2 and 20 ÷ 40 = 1/2; one factor 1/2
image B: 40 mm by 20 mm; 40 ÷ 60 = 2/3 and 20 ÷ 40 = 1/2; 2/3 is not 1/2, so B is stretched
Keeko's slip: 60 − 20 = 40 and 40 − 20 = 20, the same 20 mm taken off, but the factors differ
video_script.design: One idea: the same factor on both sides keeps the shape. Assumes dividing to compare. Wrong idea: the same length taken off keeps the shape. The three frames stay for the whole video.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks image B keeps the shape, because both sides lost the same twenty millimetres.
<bookmark mark='sub'/>Sixty take away twenty is forty, and forty take away twenty is twenty.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But taking away the same length does not give the same factor.
<bookmark mark='factors'/>The height is one half of forty, while the width is only two thirds of sixty.
<bookmark mark='stretch'/>The tiger in image B looks stretched, and only a common factor keeps the shape.
